transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-08-14
Time: 15:30 PDT
Duration: ~56 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam O'Neill (Redwood SE), Arjun Rao (Redwood SA); Priya Patel (Helix Head of ML), Carlos Vega (Eng Manager), Samir Khan (Data Scientist), Ava Li (Product)

Summary/Notes (auto): quick align on POC scope and Q-eval plan, agree on golden prompts and regression approach — Redwood to deliver playbook and benchmarks sheet

[00:00] Maya: hey everyone thanks for making time, I'll kick off, we just want to align on success criteria and how we'll measure quality during the POC — and get the sample data pipeline scoped.
[00:22] Priya: yep thanks, happy to be here. high level for us is two things: 1) match accuracy on extraction/parsing tasks, and 2) keep hallucination to a very low rate for customer-facing summaries, like under 2% ideally.
[00:38] Liam: okay great, can you unpack "accuracy" — is that exact token match, F1, or human-judged?
[00:45] Priya: good question. for entity extraction we do F1 over labeled ground truth. for summarization we want a human-evaluated correctness label plus a hallucination flag.
[01:05] Carlos: also we have a hard latency constraint — p95 end-to-end under 600ms for single-request inference from our product, because we surface results in the UI.
[01:20] Maya: noted, so success criteria draft: F1 >= 0.86 on extraction; human-correctness >= 92% on summaries; hallucination <= 2%; p95 latency <= 600ms; and cost goal to be discussed. sound reasonable?
[01:40] Priya: that's in the ballpark, we may flex cost if latency is hit.
[02:01] Samir: one more - we also want format fidelity, like JSON schema adherence for the structured outputs; failures there are a blocker.
[02:16] Arjun: ok we'll bake format checks into the regression suite — schema validation, field presence, correct types.
[02:30] Ava: timeline question: how fast can we run the baseline and iterate?
[02:38] Liam: we usually do a baseline run within 3 business days of getting a dataset sample — it's a small run (50-100 requests) to validate kernels, model variants, and latency. full POC benchmarks (10k-ish samples) take about a week of runs depending on parallelism.
[03:00] Carlos: about dataset size — our production has about 12M rows per month but the POC will sample ~10k records to represent typical payloads. is that enough?
[03:15] Liam: 10k is fine for quality evaluation if it's representative. for throughput/scale we also want a synthetic load test that mimics your concurrency profile — what's your typical concurrency?
[03:30] Priya: spikes up to 400 concurrent requests during batch windows, but user-facing is more like 20-40 concurrent.
[03:41] Liam: ok, for performance we'll simulate both 50 and 400 concurrent profiles to see batching behavior and latencies.
[03:55] Maya: let's switch to the quality eval plan — golden prompts, regression tests, and hallucination checks. Liam, can you run that?
[04:05] Liam: sure. high level approach: 1) construct a "golden prompt" set per use case — these are deterministic prompts with expected canonical outputs; 2) a regression suite with edge-case and format tests; 3) automated hallucination detection heuristics + human spot checks; 4) scoring rubric that combines automated metrics and human judgments.
[04:32] Priya: interesting — how do you detect hallucinations automatically?
[04:36] Liam: we use a mix: entity cross-checks versus ground truth, factuality classifiers for closed-domain data, and structural checks (like unexpected keys or impossible values). those are flagged for human review. it's not perfect but it surfaces likely problems.
[04:53] Samir: do you run a reranker or n-best scoring to reduce hallucination?
[04:58] Liam: we can run 2-3 candidate generations and use a lightweight reranker for correctness score; that increases cost but can lower hallucination. we'll show tradeoffs in the benchmark sheet.
[05:12] Priya: about golden prompts — we can contribute 10 canonical prompts for each of our three main flows (ingest-extract, user-summary, and rerank). should those be templated with placeholders?
[05:25] Arjun: yes templating helps. we ask for concrete examples plus a small set of adversarial prompts that try to break format.
[05:36] Ava: for scoring, can you propose a single composite score we can track? product likes one KPI.
[05:42] Liam: yes, we typically create a weighted score: 40% F1/entity extraction, 30% human correctness, 20% hallucination penalty, 10% format compliance. weights can be tuned per customer.
[05:58] Priya: that makes sense, want to see how sensitive that is to threshold choices.
[06:05] Maya: we'll provide an example scoring spreadsheet that computes those metrics across runs. we'll also include a threshold gating rule: if hallucination > 5% then fail automated acceptance.
[06:20] Carlos: on security — we need logs/audit, SSO, and KMS integration if we go private. also retention policies.
[06:29] Maya: we support SOC2 controls and KMS/HSM integrations in Private; for Hosted we have configurable retention and we can provide audit log exports. I'll attach our security pack.
[06:42] Priya: can you include runbooks for the model fallback policy — if dedicated capacity isn't available, what's the automatic behavior?
[06:49] Arjun: yes, policies are configurable — fallback to a smaller model variant or to a cached response; we'll document failover behavior in the playbook.
[07:02] Samir: for regression tests, we want both unit-level (single-prompt) and dataset-level tests (statistical regressions). how do you recommend thresholding regressions?
[07:16] Liam: unit tests are binary (pass/fail), dataset-level tests we run significance tests (bootstrap) to pick up small drifts; we flag anything outside historical variance.
[07:29] Priya: please make sure pseudo-random seeds and temperature are controlled for determinism in the baseline.
[07:36] Liam: yep, baseline runs use fixed seeds and deterministic settings where possible. we record the full config.
[07:45] Ava: what's the expected cadence for scorecard updates during the 4-week pilot?
[07:50] Maya: we recommend weekly scorecards (end-of-week) plus a mid-pilot check. final evaluation at the end of week 4.
[08:01] Carlos: cost question — can you provide token-level cost estimates across model variants and with batching?
[08:07] Liam: yes the benchmark sheet will include per-token and per-request cost modelling under different batch sizes and KV cache hit rates. we'll produce a cost tier table.
[08:19] Priya: one thing we worry about is hallucination in legal text summaries — false allegations are a blocker. can you do targeted hallucination tests?
[08:29] Arjun: we'll include domain-specific hallucination probes; for legal text we cross-check named entities and assertive statements against ground truth; flagged items go to human review.
[08:40] Samir: for format checks — some of our outputs are strict JSON with nested arrays — if the model outputs stray commas or non-JSON tokens, we need automatic sanitizer logic.
[08:54] Liam: we can run a post-processor that attempts to parse and repairs common issues; but we'll also treat parse failures as regression failures.
[09:05] Priya: ok good. any special infra needs?
[09:09] Maya: for the baseline we can run on Hosted. if you need Private for compliance we can spin up a Private trial but that lengthens timeline.
[09:20] Carlos: we prefer Hosted for POC if we can get SOC2 and retention guarantees — otherwise Private later.
[09:27] Maya: understood. we'll include both hosted and private options in the write-up.
[09:33] Ava: can you indicate what minimal sample data is required for each use-case?
[09:38] Liam: recommended minimums: extraction: 2k labeled examples; summarization: 1k human-evaluated summaries + 5k unlabeled for stress testing; format tests: 200 edge-case examples. those are guidelines.
[09:58] Priya: we can start with smaller samples and expand, we'll aim to provide the initial 1k labeled subset first.
[10:08] Maya: wrap up — agreed deliverables: playbook + benchmark sheet (Redwood), initial dataset + golden prompts (Helix), baseline run and scorecard (Redwood), weekly check-ins. next call to be scheduled after Helix uploads samples.
[10:28] Priya: that works, thanks.
[10:33] Carlos: thanks everyone.
[10:36] Maya: thanks, we'll follow up with links.
